Chapter 1: Growing Up Black in America—Early Lessons and Family Roots
You know, childhood memories can feel like they hold the weight of an entire world. For a young girl coming of age in the 1950s, that world was split in two—between the busy streets of New York and the slow, sunlit days down South.
In the city, everything seemed to move at lightning speed. Apartment buildings stacked high, neighbors’ voices traveling through thin walls, and that never-ending hum of cars and buses outside your window. But every summer, the pace changed completely. Down South, the air grew heavy with the scent of magnolias, and crickets sang you to sleep at night. Family was the heart of it all—grandparents, aunts, cousins, everyone gathered around the kitchen table, swapping stories and laughter, handing down those early lessons that stick with you for a lifetime.
The difference between North and South was about so much more than just where you were on the map. In the South, segregation was everywhere. Separate schools. Separate water fountains. Constant signals about who belonged where. Even as a child, you could feel the tension in the air whenever a white neighbor strolled by, or sense how grown-ups would hush their voices and keep their heads down when certain folks were around. Now, life in the city wasn’t perfect either. The lines weren’t always as obvious, but you could still feel eyes on you—people judging, watching, making you feel different.
Through it all, family held everything together. Imagine a mother, working long hours, determined to give her children something better. She believed in the power of books, that reading could open doors, and that standing up for yourself mattered. Then there was the grandmother—gentle, wise, always ready with comfort or advice. She taught that kindness and resilience go hand in hand. These women, along with a web of relatives and close friends, formed a safety net—a community that always had your back, especially when the world outside felt cold or unfair.
School was a mix of safe haven and battleground. Some teachers believed in you, saw your potential. But more often, they looked for trouble. The books rarely told your story. Discipline came quick, and sometimes harsh. Still, there were bright spots—games in the schoolyard, secret notes between friends, and those little sparks of excitement when you learned something new. But underneath it all, you started to get the sense that the world wasn’t set up to be fair, that some doors would always be just a little harder to open.
As you grew older, the contradictions of American life got harder to ignore. On one hand, there was this hope, this promise that anyone could make it if they worked hard enough. On the other, there was the reality—being followed in stores, hearing slurs whispered as you walked by, watching people you loved bump up against invisible walls. All of it planted seeds—sometimes of doubt, sometimes of anger, but also of determination. You realized that survival wasn’t just about getting by. It meant learning to move through a system that was never really designed for everyone.
The lessons from those early years were simple, but they ran deep: trust your instincts, lean on your community, and never forget where you come from. These values became the bedrock for everything that followed, shaping not just a sense of self, but a sense of purpose. In a world that often tried to erase or diminish Black lives, holding onto family, history, and dignity was its own quiet act of resistance.
